To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
in anaesthetized rabbits the phrenic response elicited by electrical stimulation of the vagus nerve consists of an early inhibitory and a subsequent excitatory component.
in rabbits, the phrenic response evoked by electrical stimulation of afferent vagus fibres has a short latency, but is different from that in cats.
the phrenic nerve activity in rabbits is modulated by a short-latency vagally evoked inhibition and excitation.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the effects of vagal stimulation on the respiratory activity of the phrenics in rabbits.
the study of the effects of electrical stimulation of vagal afferents on the activity of the phrenical nerve.
the development of new methods for the treatment of cancer.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the phrenic responses to electrical vagal nerve stimulation are species-specific and depend on the stimulus strength and frequency.
the vagal inhibitory influence on the phrenic activity is not a general phenomenon but is limited to some specific conditions.
the phrenic response is a bilateral inhibition followed by a bilateral enhancement, the inhibition being more prominent than the enhancement.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the vagal inhibitory input to the phrenic nucleus is mediated by myelinated vagal afferent fibres.
there is a short-latency phrenico-vagal inhibitory reflex which can be elicited in rabbits by single shock stimulation of afferent vagus fibres but not in cats.
the short-latency response of the phrrenic motoneurons to single shock stimulation is not a constant feature of the respiratory system, but depends on the species studied.
The main takeaway from our work is that
, in the rabbit, the vagal afferents do not directly excite the inspiratory phrenic motoneneurones.
